assessment.nobel_worthiness: A clear invention: trapping neutral atoms in a magic-wavelength optical lattice to interrogate a narrow clock transition with many atoms at once. It pushed frequency standards to the 1e-18 regime and opened relativistic geodesy and tests of fundamental constants. It fits the 'discovery or invention' criterion cleanly, and as an experimentalist I value that the instrument is the achievement.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and first demonstrated it. Ye built the strontium lattice clock to record precision and developed the associated spectroscopy and comparison methods. A two-person prize is a fair configuration, though I rely on recollection of the history and credit from others, such as Takamoto and Hong, is not captured in the list.
assessment.maturity: Multiple independent labs (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE, NIST and others) reproduce and extend the result. The 2005 Nobel prize for the frequency comb and 2012 prize for trapped-ion control do not cover this, so recognition is timely and arguably overdue.
uncertainties: Whether the committee sees this as distinct enough from earlier frequency-metrology prizes.
Wider credit around the early lattice-clock demonstrations is not fully captured by two names; I have not independently verified the details.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene opened a new platform in which correlated insulators and superconductivity are tunable by gate voltage and twist angle. The theory identified flat bands at a magic angle, and the experiments revealed their consequences. The field it created (moire materials, twistronics) is large and still growing, and it rests on exceptionally clean materials control.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald predicted the flat bands and magic angle from continuum theory; Jarillo-Herrero led the 2018 experiments reporting correlated states and superconductivity. Theory plus experiment is a natural pairing, though experimental credit also belongs to co-authors not named here (for example the first author of the key papers), and earlier theory by others (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto) is not on the list. This makes the allocation uncertain.
assessment.maturity: Results were replicated in many groups within a few years, and the observation of related phases has been extended to other moire systems. The interpretation of the superconducting mechanism is not settled, and the topic is arguably still young, though the core discovery is secure.
uncertainties: Credit among theorists and among the experimental team is disputed or incomplete in the supplied names.
Possible prematurity relative to longer-established candidates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller 1995 proposal for quantum gates with trapped ions, and its experimental realisation with entangling gates, teleportation and small algorithms, established a leading architecture for quantum computing. The idea was original and the experimental follow-through was demanding.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller made the decisive theoretical proposal; Blatt led key early experimental demonstrations of gates and algorithms in a Paul trap. Wineland's group (already honoured in 2012) and others such as Monroe also contributed, so the experimental credit is shared and some of it was already recognised.
assessment.maturity: The approach is confirmed independently in several laboratories and has scaled to commercial devices. The 2012 prize to Wineland and Haroche and 2025 prize for superconducting circuits narrow the room somewhat; the field is mature but still evolving.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 prize and the question of who is the 'first' experimental demonstrator.
Whether the committee prefers to treat this together with other quantum-computing candidates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical detection and coherent control of single spins in diamond colour centres (NV and related) created a room-temperature quantum sensor with nanoscale resolution. It spans quantum information, magnetometry and imaging in materials and biology, and is a concept I understand from nanoscale characterisation. The importance and breadth are high.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup and Jelezko demonstrated optical detection of single NV centres and coherent control; Awschalom extended coherent spin control in diamond and silicon carbide. Lukin is also credited in the list but I leave him out because the breadth of work makes a three-person selection already difficult. The lines between 'single-spin detection', 'sensing' and 'quantum networks' blur, so allocation is not obvious.
assessment.maturity: The result is robust and reproduced worldwide, with many applications and commercial products. The compound nature of the field means different parts may mature at different speeds.
uncertainties: Whether the prize topic is single-spin detection, quantum sensing or networks.
The fourth credited person, Lukin, is excluded under the three-laureate limit and the choice is debatable.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Room-temperature tunnel magnetoresistance in magnetic tunnel junctions, and especially the large effect in crystalline MgO barriers, underlies modern hard-disk read heads and MRAM. It is a combination of discovery, a theoretical prediction and an engineering invention with big practical consequences, and the epitaxial-interface structure matters to the outcome, which I appreciate from interface microscopy.
assessment.attribution: Miyazaki's group reported large room-temperature TMR in 1995; Parkin and Yuasa demonstrated coherent tunnelling in MgO junctions in 2004; Butler predicted the effect theoretically. Moodera, who also reported room-temperature TMR in 1995, is not on the supplied list, which makes the fair allocation uncertain. I choose the three experimental names.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed and commercialised for nearly two decades. Fert and Grunberg received the 2007 prize for giant magnetoresistance, so some may see this as a continuation; timing is not an issue.
uncertainties: Moodera is absent from the credited names, and Butler's theoretical role is excluded by the three-name limit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators created a new category of matter with protected edge states, and had large conceptual impact across condensed matter. Both the prediction and the observation in HgTe quantum wells are important.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele proposed the Z2 topological insulator and quantum spin Hall effect in graphene; Molenkamp's group observed it in HgTe wells following the proposal by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang. Zhang is deceased and Bernevig and Hughes are not on this entry, so the credit does not reflect all decisive contributions. Other candidate entries credit Xue instead, indicating overlapping topics.
assessment.maturity: The state is confirmed by multiple experiments, including 3D topological insulators and ARPES evidence. The field is mature and widely accepted, with practical applications still limited.
uncertainties: Incomplete credit: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang are not on this entry.
Overlap with other topological-insulator candidates and the 2016 Nobel Prize for topological phases.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The observation of a high-mobility two-dimensional electron gas at the LaAlO3/SrTiO3 interface showed that polar discontinuity at an oxide interface can create new electronic states, including superconductivity and magnetism. It launched oxide electronics. I disclose that my group has worked on oxygen vacancies and interface structure in this very system, so I ought to be cautious about my own judgement.
assessment.attribution: Ohtomo and Hwang reported the 2004 observation; Mannhart and colleagues showed the tunable superconductivity and the gate control. I left Mannhart out to keep a two-person set that follows the original discovery, but this is arguable.
assessment.maturity: The effect is reproduced widely, but its origin is still debated, since oxygen vacancies, cation intermixing and polar-catastrophe mechanisms each contribute, which is partly why my own work has been relevant. The interpretation is not fully stable, and recognition may be premature.
uncertainties: Ongoing disagreement over the role of oxygen vacancies and intermixing versus polar discontinuity.
A possible conflict of interest because of my own work on this system.
Allocation of credit between Ohtomo, Hwang and Mannhart.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum cascade laser was a genuinely new type of semiconductor laser, in which designed band-structure engineering of intersubband transitions in a heterostructure gives emission set by layer thickness rather than the material. It opened the mid-infrared and terahertz ranges for sensing and spectroscopy, and is a clear 'invention' with the practical impact the criterion invites.
assessment.attribution: Faist and Capasso led the 1994 demonstration at Bell Labs and Cho supplied the molecular-beam epitaxy growth; Sirtori and others in the team are not credited here, and Kazarinov and Suris proposed the idea theoretically in 1971, so the credit allocation is not simple.
assessment.maturity: The device is mature, with broad independent confirmation and extensive commercial use. It could be recognised now without concern about prematurity.
uncertainties: Missing names (for example Sirtori and Kazarinov and Suris) complicate attribution.
Whether the committee considers this physics or engineering.
